item.title: Does an Electric Car Actually Save You Money?
item.dc:creator: SixtyEight95
item.description:
Electric car fans say you’ll save a fortune on gas. Skeptics say EVs cost more and lose value fast. They’re both partly right. To settle it, we compared the full cost of owning an EV, a gas car, and a hybrid of the same size and class, per year.

The short answer

An EV saves you about $1,728 a year on fuel and maintenance (for a medium sedan). But it loses value so much faster that a new EV costs $3,080 more per year to own than a comparable gas sedan. In SUVs, it’s roughly a tie. And in every class, a hybrid was cheapest.

How we compared them

We used AAA’s 2026 Your Driving Costs study, which averages the top-selling 2026 models in each class and adds up everything it costs to own one for five years at 15,000 miles a year:

  • Fuel or charging
  • Maintenance and repairs, including tires
  • Depreciation: how much value the car loses
  • Insurance (full coverage)
  • License, registration, and taxes, including the extra EV fees most states now charge
  • Finance charges: interest on the car loan

That puts every vehicle on the same footing: dollars per year.

The results

Total cost per year, new 2026 models, 15,000 miles a year. Source: AAA.
Class Electric Gas Hybrid EV vs gas
Medium sedan $13,662 $10,582 $10,204 EV costs $3,080 more
Compact SUV $11,888 $11,656 $11,201 EV costs $232 more
Medium SUV $14,332 $14,431 $13,698 EV saves $99
Pickup truck $17,414 $16,626 $16,117 EV costs $788 more

Where EVs win: running costs

The EV advantage is real. For a medium sedan, charging cost about $712 a year versus $2,215 for gas, and maintenance was cheaper too (no oil changes, fewer moving parts, and brakes that last longer thanks to regenerative braking).

One big catch: where you charge. AAA’s EV fuel costs line up with home electricity prices, which average about $0.19 per kWh nationally. Public fast chargers typically cost around $0.45 per kWh, about 2.3 times more. If you can’t charge at home and rely on fast chargers, a medium sedan’s charging bill rises to roughly $1,661 a year: still less than gas, but most of the savings are gone.

Where EVs lose: owning costs

The biggest single cost of owning any new car is depreciation, the value it loses while you own it. For EVs, it’s brutal. AAA puts a new electric medium sedan’s depreciation at $6,786 a year, versus $3,330 for gas. Fast-improving battery technology and price cuts on new EVs make used ones worth less.

EVs also tend to cost more to insure (they’re pricier to repair), most states now charge an extra annual EV registration fee (often $100 to $250) to make up for lost gas-tax revenue, and a pricier car means more loan interest. And as of September 30, 2025, the $7,500 federal EV tax credit is gone.

So who should buy an EV?

The numbers point to a few clear cases where an EV makes financial sense:

  • You can charge at home. That’s where the fuel savings come from.
  • You drive a lot. More miles means more fuel savings to offset the extra ownership costs.
  • You keep cars a long time. Depreciation is heaviest in the first few years. Keep the car 10 years and the per-year cost of that early drop shrinks.
  • You buy used. The first owner already took the big depreciation hit. A used EV can capture the running-cost savings without paying for the steepest part of the value drop.
  • You’re shopping SUVs, not sedans. The gap is smallest there.

If saving money is the top priority and none of those fit, the data say: buy a hybrid. It beat both EVs and gas cars in every class AAA measured.

The fine print

  • These are averages across top-selling models. A specific EV with a big discount, or a gas guzzler, can change the answer.
  • Five-year ownership is AAA’s assumption. Longer ownership generally helps EVs.
  • Electricity and gas prices vary a lot by state. Cheap power and expensive gas favor EVs.
  • Public charging prices vary by network and membership; ours is a typical 2026 figure.
  • This post is about money. Whether EVs are better for the environment is a separate question, and our follow-up post tackles it.

The bottom line

EVs really are cheaper to run. But “cheaper to run” isn’t “cheaper to own.” Buying new, without the old federal tax credit, an EV costs about the same as a gas SUV and more than a gas sedan, because it loses value so fast. If you can charge at home, drive a lot, keep cars for years, or buy used, the math tilts toward electric. Otherwise, a hybrid is the money winner.

How we did this. Annual costs are from AAA’s Your Driving Costs 2026 study (EV, gas, and hybrid comparison for medium sedans, compact SUVs, medium SUVs, and pickups; 15,000 miles a year, five-year ownership, full-coverage insurance). Home electricity is the BLS average U.S. price per kWh over the last 12 months, via FRED. The public fast-charging price is a typical 2026 figure from industry price trackers. AAA Your Driving Costs 2026

item.title: Why Are Hospital Bills So Insanely Expensive?
item.dc:creator: SixtyEight95
item.description:
A night in the hospital can cost more than a used car. A routine birth can come with a bill in the thousands, even with insurance. Everyone knows American hospital care is expensive. We wanted to know how expensive, compared with what, and why.

The short answer

Hospital prices have grown about 17.3× since 1980, while pay grew 4.7×. A hip replacement that private insurers paid $29,006 for in the U.S. cost $7,681 in Germany.

The biggest reasons: private insurers pay hospitals about 254% of what Medicare pays, hospitals have merged into local near-monopolies, about a quarter of hospital spending goes to administration, and hospital “list prices” are inflated far beyond cost.

45 years of hospital prices, in hours of work

Like our other cost-of-living stories, we measured hospital prices against what the average worker earns. If a hospital service took 100 hours of work to pay for in 1980, here’s how many hours the same service has taken since.

Hospital care now takes about 3.7 times as many hours of work as it did in 1980. Unlike college tuition, which has started getting easier to afford, hospital prices have stayed near their peak.

The same procedure, around the world

The International Federation of Health Plans compared what private insurers paid for the same hospital procedures in nine countries in 2022. These are actual payments, not list prices.

Hover over any dot to see the country. The U.S. is the most expensive for every procedure. The biggest gap of all is heart bypass surgery: $89,094 in the U.S., versus $16,936 in Germany and $15,183 in Spain.

Median price paid by private insurers, 2022. Source: iFHP/HCCI 2024 report.
Procedure U.S. UK Germany Australia Spain
Heart bypass $89,094 $25,804 $16,936 $17,741 $15,183
Hip replacement $29,006 $14,849 $7,681 $14,986 $6,780
Knee replacement $26,340 $15,216 $8,522 $13,609 $6,600
C-section $13,601 $8,910 $2,419 $7,742 $2,807
Appendectomy $13,560 $3,950 $3,980 $4,268 $2,622
Vaginal birth $8,655 $3,002 $1,361 $5,318 $2,175

Why: the four big reasons

1. Private insurance pays hospitals more than double what Medicare pays

The same hospital, the same procedure, very different prices depending on who’s paying. RAND studied claims from employer health plans across the country and found that in 2022, they paid hospitals 254% of what Medicare would have paid for the same care. In some states it was over 300%.

Medicare sets its prices. Private insurers have to negotiate them, and often they don’t have much leverage, which leads to reason two.

2. Hospitals have merged into local near-monopolies

Over the past few decades, hospitals have bought each other up. KFF found that in 47% of U.S. metro areas, the entire hospital market is controlled by just one or two health systems. When an insurer has to include a hospital system in its network because there’s no alternative, that system can charge more. Research consistently finds that hospital mergers raise prices, without clear improvements in quality.

3. A quarter of the budget goes to paperwork

Billing in the U.S. is complicated: hundreds of insurers, each with its own rules, codes, and approval processes. One study found that administration took about 25% of U.S. hospital budgets, about twice the share in Canada or Scotland. (The study’s authors support a single-payer system, but the gap they measured is large under any interpretation.)

4. The “list price” is mostly fiction

Every hospital has a “chargemaster,” a master list of prices. These list prices bear little resemblance to what care costs. A study of Medicare cost data found the average hospital listed $4.32 for every $1 of its actual costs, and up to about 28 times cost for CT scans.

Medicare and insurers rarely pay list prices. The people who often get billed them are the uninsured and patients treated out of network, the ones with the least power to negotiate.

The human cost

About 20 million adults owe significant medical debt (over $250), totaling at least $220 billion, according to KFF. Hospital bills are a big part of that.

The fine print

  • Different years. Country prices and the Medicare comparison are from 2022, the administrative cost study is from 2011 data, and the list price study from 2013. The patterns have held up in later research, but the exact numbers have moved.
  • Country prices are medians of what private insurers paid, converted to U.S. dollars by the report’s authors. Public systems in some countries may pay less.
  • “Hours of work” uses the government’s hospital services price index and the average worker’s hourly pay before taxes. It tracks how prices changed, not any one bill.
  • What you personally pay depends on your insurance, deductible, and whether the hospital is in network.

The bottom line

Health economists have been saying it for decades: American health care is expensive mainly because the prices are higher, not because Americans get far more care. For hospitals, private insurers pay far more than Medicare, merged hospital systems have the leverage to keep it that way, billing complexity adds a heavy layer of cost, and inflated list prices land hardest on the people least able to pay.

How we did this. Procedure prices are from the International Federation of Health Plans and Health Care Cost Institute’s International Healthcare Cost Comparison Report 2024 (2022 data), read from the report’s charts. The Medicare comparison is from RAND’s hospital price transparency study (Round 5.1). Market concentration is from KFF. Administrative costs are from Himmelstein et al., Health Affairs (2014). List price markups are from Bai & Anderson, Health Affairs (2016). Medical debt is from KFF’s analysis of Census survey data. The hours-of-work trend uses the CPI for hospital services (BLS series CUUR0000SEMD) and average hourly earnings of production and nonsupervisory employees, both via FRED. iFHP/HCCI report · RAND · KFF on markets · KFF on medical debt

item.title: Insulin Costs About $5 a Vial to Make. Here’s What Countries Actually Pay.
item.dc:creator: SixtyEight95
item.description:
You’ve probably seen the claim: insulin costs a few dollars to make, but Americans pay hundreds. Insulin was discovered more than 100 years ago, and its inventors famously sold the patent to the University of Toronto for $1 each so it would stay affordable. So how did a vial end up costing more than a car payment?

We dug into the research to see what insulin really costs to make, what other wealthy countries pay, and what the U.S. number actually means.

The short answer

A vial of insulin (1,000 units) costs an estimated $3 to $9 to make, including a profit margin. In 2022, other wealthy countries paid an average of $24 per vial. The U.S. list price averaged $227.

But that list price is not what insurers actually paid. After secret discounts, the U.S. paid about $54, still about 2.3 times other countries. And a lot has changed since 2022.

What it costs to make

In 2018, researchers published a detailed estimate in BMJ Global Health of what insulin would cost if many companies competed to make it, the way they do for generic pills. They added up the raw ingredients, filling and packaging the vials, building factories, getting regulatory approval, shipping, and a 20% margin for overhead and profit.

One 10 mL vial = 1,000 units. Source: Gotham, Barber & Hill, BMJ Global Health (2018).
Type of insulin Estimated price per vial
Regular human insulin $3.29 – $4.86
NPH (human) $3.35 – $4.93
Glargine (Lantus-type) $5.32 – $7.38
Lispro (Humalog-type) $6.51 – $8.87
Aspart (Novolog-type) $6.50 – $8.86

So yes, the viral claim holds up: insulin is cheap to make. Even the newer, longer-lasting insulins come in under $10 a vial.

What these estimates don’t include: the original research that created each insulin, the pharmacy’s markup, or insurance. They’re an estimate of what a competitive market could charge, not what any company actually spends.

What wealthy countries pay

The RAND Corporation compared insulin prices in the U.S. and 33 other wealthy countries using 2022 sales data. These are the prices drugmakers charge before discounts, averaged across all the insulin each country uses.

The U.S. isn’t just a little higher. At $227 per vial, it was about 9.7 times the average of the other 33 countries (RAND’s careful like-for-like comparison). Canada, often the go-to comparison, was $38.

Notice something else, though: every country pays well above the cost to make it. The UK pays roughly 2 to 7 times the estimated production cost. Everyone pays a markup. The U.S. markup was just in a different league.

Why the U.S. sticker price was never the real price

Here’s the part that rarely makes the viral posts. In the U.S., drugmakers set a high list price, then pay big secret rebates to the companies that manage insurance drug plans (called pharmacy benefit managers, or PBMs) in exchange for being covered. RAND estimates those discounts knocked about 76% off the U.S. list price.

So who paid the $227? Often the people with the least bargaining power: the uninsured, and people in high-deductible plans, whose out-of-pocket costs are frequently based on the list price. That’s how insulin became a symbol of American health care, even though insurers were paying far less.

Researchers still argue over who’s to blame for the system. Some point to drugmakers raising list prices; others point to middlemen who earn more when list prices and rebates are both high. Either way, even after the discounts, the U.S. still paid about 2.3 times what other wealthy countries paid.

What’s changed since 2022

The RAND data is from 2022, and the U.S. insulin market has changed a lot since then:

  • List price cuts. In 2023, Eli Lilly cut list prices for its main insulins by about 70%. Novo Nordisk’s cuts of 65–75% and Sanofi’s 78% cut to Lantus took effect in January 2024.
  • $35 caps. Since 2023, people on Medicare pay no more than $35 a month for insulin. Some states, including California, cap it for many private plans too, and the big makers offer $35 programs.
  • New low-cost insulin. In January 2026, California’s CalRx program and the nonprofit drugmaker Civica launched a long-acting insulin at no more than $55 for five pens, about $11 a pen. That works out to about $37 per 1,000 units, right in line with what Canada paid in 2022.

These changes don’t show up in the 2022 numbers, so today’s U.S. list prices are lower than our chart shows.

The fine print

  • Different years, different sources. The cost estimate is from 2018; the country prices are from 2022.
  • Country prices are averages across all the insulin each country buys, so a country that uses more of the newer insulins will look a bit pricier.
  • U.S. discounts are estimated. Rebates are confidential, so RAND applied an average discount.
  • No country’s price includes the pharmacy’s markup or taxes. What patients pay at the counter can differ.

The bottom line

Insulin really is cheap to make, roughly $3 to $9 a vial. Other wealthy countries pay a few times that. The U.S. list price was about ten times higher than theirs, but it mostly functioned as a starting point for secret discounts, and the people who paid it were the ones least able to. After a wave of price cuts, caps, and new low-cost options since 2023, the gap is closing. But it hasn’t closed.

How we did this. Country prices are from RAND’s report Comparing Insulin Prices in the United States to Other Countries: Updated Results Using 2022 Data (Mulcahy & Schwam, 2024), which analyzed IQVIA sales data for the U.S. and 33 OECD countries (Table A.5, average gross price per 100 units, all insulins, multiplied by 10 for a 1,000-unit vial). The U.S. after-discount price applies RAND’s 76% gross-to-net estimate. Production cost estimates are from Gotham, Barber & Hill, “Production costs and potential prices for biosimilars of human insulin and insulin analogues,” BMJ Global Health (2018), Table 1. RAND report · BMJ Global Health study

item.title: Buying a Home, Measured in Hours of Work
item.dc:creator: SixtyEight95
item.description:
“Nobody can afford a house anymore” might be the most repeated money complaint in America. We wanted to know how true it is, so we measured the cost of a home the way it actually feels: in hours of work.

The short answer

The mortgage on a typical new home takes about 71 hours of work a month today. That’s a lot more than in 2021 (56 hours), but less than in 1990 (96 hours). The monthly payment isn’t the worst it’s ever been. The down payment is the bigger wall.

What “hours of work” means

We take the monthly mortgage payment on a median-priced new home and divide it by what the average worker earns per hour, before taxes. The answer is how many hours of work it takes to cover the payment each month.

For scale: a full-time job is about 173 hours a month. So today’s 71 hours is roughly 41% of one person’s pay before taxes. (Many households have two earners, which makes it easier, but we stick to one so the comparison is the same in every year.)

50 years of mortgage payments, in hours

Hover to see the price, the rate, and the payment behind each point.

The worst moment was the end of 1981, when mortgage rates were near 18% and the payment took 124 hours a month. The best was 2011, at 49 hours, with rates around 4%.

Interest rates are the big lever

Notice what happened between 2021 and 2023. Home prices relative to pay barely moved, but the payment went from 56 hours to 87 hours of work a month. That jump was almost all interest rates, which went from about 3% to 6.8%.

To see how much rates matter: today’s median new home costs about $406,900. At today’s rate (about 6.4%), the monthly payment is about $2,280. At 2021’s rate, the same house would cost $1,536 a month. Same house, $744 a month difference.

The catch: getting in the door

The monthly payment is only half the story. Before you get a mortgage, you need a down payment, and that depends on the price of the house, not the interest rate.

A 10% down payment on a typical new home is about $40,690 today. That’s 7.3 months of the average worker’s full pay, before taxes and before spending a dime on anything else. In 1985 it was 5.6 months.

That’s why buying feels so out of reach even though the monthly payment isn’t at a record: the house itself costs more years of pay than it did in the 1980s, so the savings hurdle is higher.

Snapshot by year

Year Median new home Mortgage rate Monthly payment Hours of work / month 10% down, in months of pay
1975 $39,275 9% $286 60 4.8
1981 $68,950 16.6% $867 116 5.4
1985 $84,275 12.4% $805 92 5.6
1990 $122,300 10.1% $977 96 6.9
2000 $167,550 8.1% $1,112 79 6.9
2006 $243,750 6.4% $1,374 82 8.4
2012 $244,400 3.7% $1,007 51 7.2
2019 $320,250 3.9% $1,365 58 7.9
2021 $383,000 3% $1,446 56 8.5
2023 $426,525 6.8% $2,505 87 8.5
2026 (so far) $405,100 6.4% $2,280 71 7.3

The fine print

  • Principal and interest only. Property taxes and homeowners insurance aren’t included, and insurance in particular has gotten much more expensive in many states. Real monthly costs are higher than shown.
  • Newly built homes. The government’s long-running median price series covers new homes. Existing homes follow a similar trend, but prices differ.
  • National medians. A typical home in San Francisco and one in Toledo are very different stories.
  • One average earner, before taxes. Your own hours depend on your pay and your household.

The bottom line

Monthly mortgage payments are high compared with the cheap-money years of 2010–2021, but not compared with the 1980s and early ’90s. What’s genuinely harder now is the price of entry: the down payment takes more of a paycheck than it did a generation ago. If rates come down, the monthly payment gets easier fast. The down payment problem only gets easier if pay grows faster than home prices.

How we did this. Home prices are the median sales price of new houses sold in the U.S. (Census Bureau and HUD). Mortgage rates are Freddie Mac’s 30-year fixed average. Pay is average hourly earnings of production and nonsupervisory employees (about 80% of private-sector workers) from the Bureau of Labor Statistics. All series come from FRED. We assume 10% down and a 30-year fixed loan at that quarter’s average rate. Hours of work = monthly payment ÷ hourly pay. “Today” is the average of the latest four quarters (through Q3 2026).
